When a first verb needs a second one to complete its meaning, link them with zu + Infinitiv: Ich hoffe, Deutsch zu lernen. The pattern also follows certain adjectives (Es ist wichtig, …) and nouns (Ich habe Lust, …). Separable verbs tuck zu between the prefix and the stem: anzurufen.

When a first (conjugated) verb needs a second verb to complete its meaning, the second verb goes to the end as an Infinitiv, introduced by zu.
Structure: Verb 1 (conjugated) … zu + Infinitiv (at the end of the clause). A comma usually separates the two parts when the zu-phrase has its own elements.
Ich habe vergessen, den Lehrer anzurufen.
Wir planen, nach Deutschland zu fahren.

Jab pehla verb apne aap mein poora nahi hota aur usko doosre verb ki zaroorat hoti hai, to doosra verb Infinitiv (dictionary form) mein end mein jaata hai, aur uske pehle zu lagta hai. Aksar comma dono hisson ko alag karta hai — khaas kar jab zu-phrase ke saath aur bhi words hon.
These thirteen verbs are the most common triggers for zu + Infinitiv at B1. Learn them as a set — whenever one appears, expect zu + Infinitiv to follow.
Ich habe vergessen, den Lehrer anzurufen.
Wir planen, nach Deutschland zu fahren.
Ich bitte dich, leiser zu sprechen.
Ich empfehle dir, früh zu buchen.
Er fängt an, Deutsch zu üben.
Yeh 13 verbs B1 mein sabse zyada zu + Infinitiv ke saath aate hain. Inhe ek group ki tarah yaad rakho — jab bhi in mein se koi verb aaye, samajh jao ki uske baad zu + Infinitiv aayega.
A group of adjectives after Es ist … also trigger zu + Infinitiv: wichtig (important), schwer (hard), leicht (easy), sinnvoll (sensible), möglich (possible).
Es ist wichtig, genug zu schlafen.
Es ist schwer, Deutsch perfekt zu sprechen.
Es ist leicht, diese Regel zu verstehen.
Es ist sinnvoll, früh zu buchen.
Es ist möglich, das bis Freitag zu schaffen.
"Es ist + adjective" ke baad bhi zu + Infinitiv aata hai — jaise wichtig (zaroori), schwer (mushkil), leicht (aasan), sinnvoll (samajhdaari ki baat) aur möglich (possible).
Certain nouns after Ich habe … behave the same way: Lust (desire/mood), Zeit (time), Angst (fear), die Möglichkeit (the possibility).
Ich habe Lust, ins Kino zu gehen.
Ich habe keine Zeit, jetzt zu telefonieren.
Sie hat Angst, den Fehler zu wiederholen.
Wir haben die Möglichkeit, früher zu fliegen.
"Ich habe + noun" ke baad bhi zu + Infinitiv aata hai — jaise Lust (man karna), Zeit (time), Angst (dar) aur die Möglichkeit (chance).
Trennbare Verben: zu geht zwischen Präfix und Verb
With separable verbs, zu is inserted between the separable prefix and the verb stem, and the whole thing is written as ONE word.
Normal verb: lernen → zu lernen (zu stays separate, before the verb). Separable verb: aufstehen → aufzustehen (zu slots inside, between auf and stehen).
The separable prefix always stays attached to the verb — zu never comes before it as a separate word. zu fernsehen is wrong; fernzusehen is correct.

Trennbare verbs mein zu prefix aur verb ke BEECH mein aata hai, aur poora ek hi word banta hai: auf + zu + stehen = aufzustehen. Prefix hamesha verb ke saath hi rehta hai — usse pehle zu alag word ki tarah kabhi nahi aata.
These four mistakes appear constantly at B1 — because in English "to" often comes before the FIRST verb, not the second, learners forget zu entirely or place it in the wrong spot.
zu is required before the second verb — it never disappears.
The second verb must be an Infinitiv with zu, not a conjugated form.
Ich habe Lust ins Kino gehen.
Ich habe Lust, ins Kino zu gehen.
Noun triggers like Lust also need zu before the Infinitiv.
planen needs zu before the Infinitiv. (The comma is optional when the zu-phrase is bare, but required once it carries its own elements, as here.)
Yeh galtiyaan isliye hoti hain kyunki English mein "to" pehle verb ke pehle aata hai, German mein zu doosre verb ke pehle aata hai. Isliye zu bhoolna ya galat jagah lagana sabse aam galti hai.
Word order: Verb 1 (conjugated, position 2) … [comma] … rest of the zu-phrase … zu + Infinitiv (always last).
Quick decision guide — ask yourself two questions:
Does the first verb need another verb to complete its meaning?
Is that second verb separable (has a prefix like an-, auf-, mit-, fern-)?
Yes → put zu between the prefix and the verb: anzurufen, aufzustehen.
Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, möchten) are the one big exception — they take a plain Infinitiv with NO zu: Ich kann kommen. not Ich kann zu kommen.

Word order: Verb 1 (position 2) … comma … baaki phrase … zu + Infinitiv (hamesha end mein). Decision guide: (1) Kya pehle verb ko doosre verb ki zaroorat hai? Haan to zu + Infinitiv. (2) Kya woh verb trennbar hai? Haan to zu prefix aur verb ke beech mein jaata hai. Modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, möchten) is rule se bahar hain — unke baad plain Infinitiv aata hai, zu nahi.

b1-10-passiv-praesens: Das Auto wird repariert. Die Tür wird geöffnet. Hier wird nicht geraucht. This chapter shifts the focus from WHO does something to WHAT happens — the present passive, built from werden + Partizip II, for announcements, instructions, and formal descriptions where the actor is unknown, unimportant, or simply obvious.

At the hairdresser's, Timo asks what's being done to his hair today, and Frau Bruns answers step by step — washed, then cut, coloured only on request. The present passive puts the process front and centre, not who's doing it.

Active sentences ask WHO does something: Der Koch kocht das Essen. Passive sentences ask WHAT HAPPENS: Das Essen wird gekocht. Build it with werden (conjugated, Position 2) + Partizip II (Satzende) — used when the actor is unknown, unimportant, or simply obvious: rules, announcements, instructions, newspapers.

In a Dativ relative clause, the relative pronoun is the INDIRECT OBJECT — it answers Wem? (To whom?).
Das ist der Mann. Ich helfe dem Mann. → Das ist der Mann, dem ich helfe.
Das ist die Frau. Ich danke der Frau. → Das ist die Frau, der ich danke.
Das ist das Kind. Ich gebe dem Kind ein Geschenk. → Das ist das Kind, dem ich ein Geschenk gebe.
Das sind die Studenten. Ich erkläre den Studenten die Aufgabe. → Das sind die Studenten, denen ich die Aufgabe erkläre.
Dativ relative clause mein relative pronoun INDIRECT OBJECT hota hai — yeh Wem? (Kisko?) ka jawab deta hai.

Every German adjective ending answers ONE question: has the gender/case already been shown? After der/die/das the article already shows it, so the adjective barely needs to — weak (der große Hund). After ein/kein/mein… the article is ambiguous in three spots, so the adjective steps in there — mixed (ein großer Hund). With no article at all, the adjective must show everything itself — strong (großer Hund). Same word, same meaning — the ending just fills whatever gap the article leaves.

German always needs to show gender, number, and case exactly once per noun phrase. If the article already shows it clearly, the adjective ending shrinks. If the article does not show enough, the adjective ending grows to compensate.
Don't memorize three tables — ask ONE question every time: how much information does the article in front of me already carry?

German hamesha gender, number, aur case ek hi baar dikhana chahta hai. Agar article pehle se saaf dikhata hai, to adjective ki ending chhoti ho jaati hai. Agar article kaafi nahi dikhata, to adjective ki ending badi ho jaati hai.
After der/die/das/die, the article already carries the full signal, so the adjective mostly just adds -e or -en.
der/die/das/die ke baad, article pehle se poora signal deta hai, isliye adjective bas -e ya -en jodta hai.

After ein/eine/ein, kein, mein/dein/sein/ihr/unser/euer, the article is ambiguous in exactly three spots (masc. Nom., neut. Nom./Akk.) — the adjective fills those gaps with a strong ending; everywhere else it matches weak.
Only three cells differ from weak declension: masc. Nom. (-er instead of -e) and neut. Nom./Akk. (-es instead of -e). Everywhere else, mixed = weak.
ein/kein/mein… ke baad, article sirf teen jagah ambiguous hai (masc. Nom., neut. Nom./Akk.) — adjective un jagahon ko strong ending se bharta hai; baaki jagah weak jaisa hi hota hai.
With no article at all, the adjective alone must carry gender, number, AND case — so it takes almost the same endings a der-word would.
The strong ending mirrors der/die/das/den almost exactly — the adjective steps into the article's shoes.
Bina article ke, sirf adjective ko gender, number, AUR case dikhana padta hai — isliye yeh lagbhag der-word jaisi ending leta hai.
Same adjective, same noun, three endings — because three different amounts of information are already on the table.
Same adjective, same noun, teen endings — kyunki teeno mein article pehle se alag-alag kitni jaankari de raha hai.

Strong declension: no article, masculine Nominativ needs -er.

A hungry fox stood under a tall tree. On the branch sat a proud crow with a large piece of cheese in its sharp beak. The clever fox praised the proud crow's beautiful voice. Although the small fox lied, the vain crow believed every word. He opened his sharp beak to sing a loud song. The large piece fell directly into the clever fox's hungry mouth. The disappointed crow left silently. That's why the old fable's simple moral reads: flattering words often come from false friends.

Futur I is one structure — werden (conjugated, Position 2) + Infinitiv (Satzende) — doing four different jobs: a future plan (Ich werde nächstes Jahr studieren.), a prediction (Morgen wird es regnen.), a promise (Ich werde dir helfen.), or an assumption about right now (Er wird jetzt zu Hause sein.). Präsens works for plain future plans too — Futur I adds emphasis or certainty.

The lesson is FUTUR I (B1 level only): werden (conjugated: ich werde, du wirst, er/sie/es wird, wir werden, ihr werdet, sie/Sie werden) + Infinitiv at the very end of the clause, used for (1) future plans, (2) predictions, (3) promises, and (4) present-moment assumptions (Vermutung). Präsens is equally correct for plain future plans — Futur I is chosen for emphasis, clarity, or when the four uses above call for it. Both are grammatically correct for future plans. Präsens is the everyday spoken choice; Futur I adds emphasis, certainty, or clarity — and is required for pure predictions/assumptions about things with no time marker.
Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahren.

Future plans ke liye dono sahi hain. Rozmarra bolchaal mein log aksar Präsens hi use karte hain, khaas kar jab saath mein koi time word ho (Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin). Futur I tab aata hai jab tum emphasis ya certainty dena chahte ho, ya jab sirf prediction ya assumption bata rahe ho.
Time expressions and other middle-field elements sit BETWEEN werden and the final infinitive — never after the infinitive.
Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahren.
Ich werde nach Berlin fahren morgen.
Time expressions aur baaki saari cheezein werden aur end wale Infinitiv ke beech mein aati hain. Infinitiv ke baad kuch nahi aata — woh sentence ka aakhri word hota hai.

Two conjugated verbs can never stand together. Futur I has exactly ONE conjugated verb (werden) and the rest as infinitives at the end. This double-infinitive form is beyond B1 — just avoid the mistake for now.
werden must agree with its subject — ich takes werde, not wird (which is for er/sie/es).

Both structures answer the same question — Why? For what purpose? — but the choice is mechanical: ask who performs both actions. Same person in both clauses? Use um … zu + Infinitiv (Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten.). Two different people? A purpose clause answers Why? For what purpose? Both um...zu and damit express the SAME kind of goal — the choice between them is purely mechanical.
Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten.
Ich lerne Deutsch, damit ich in Deutschland arbeiten kann.
Purpose clause batata hai ki koi kaam kis liye kiya jaa raha hai. um...zu aur damit dono SAME tarah ka goal express karte hain.
um + Infinitiv + zu (bare infinitive, no separate subject) — used ONLY when the same person performs both actions.
Anna spart Geld, um ein Auto zu kaufen.
Rohan fährt früher los, um pünktlich anzukommen.
um + Infinitiv + zu (bina alag subject ke) — sirf tab use hota hai jab dono kaam ek hi insaan kar raha ho.
damit + full subordinate clause with its own subject and finite verb at the end — used when the two clauses have DIFFERENT subjects.
Anna spricht langsam, damit Rohan alles versteht.
Er schreibt alles auf, damit er nichts vergisst.
damit can technically be used even with the same subject, but um...zu is preferred and more natural whenever the subjects match.
damit + poora subordinate clause apne subject aur finite verb ke saath end mein — jab dono clauses ke ALAG subjects hon.
The exact same goal, expressed two ways — only the subject test changes which structure is grammatically required.
Ich spare Geld, um ein Auto zu kaufen.
Ich spare Geld, damit meine Schwester studieren kann.
Bilkul wahi goal, do tareekon se express kiya gaya — sirf subject test yeh tay karta hai ki kaun sa structure chahiye.
One question decides the structure every time.
Memory trick: ONE person → um...zu. TWO people → damit.
Ek sawaal har baar structure tay karta hai: Dono kaam kaun kar raha hai? Ek hi insaan → um...zu. Alag-alag log → damit.
These five mistakes come from giving um...zu its own subject, dropping zu, using the wrong subject test, or blending the two structures.
Ich lerne Deutsch, um ich in Deutschland arbeiten.
Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten.
um...zu never has its own conjugated subject — only zu + bare Infinitiv.
Ich spare Geld, damit ein Auto kaufen.
Ich spare Geld, um ein Auto zu kaufen.
damit always needs a full clause with its own subject and finite verb — here the subject is the same, so um...zu is required instead.
Anna spricht langsam, um Rohan alles versteht.
Anna spricht langsam, damit Rohan alles versteht.
The subjects are different (Anna vs. Rohan) — damit is required, not um...zu.
Ich komme früh, um pünktlich zu sein. / Ich komme früh, damit alle pünktlich beginnen können.
"um dass" is not a valid German structure — it blends um...zu and dass incorrectly.
um zu arbeiten (same subject) / damit sie arbeiten kann (different subject)
damit is never followed directly by zu + Infinitiv — it always introduces a full clause with a conjugated verb.
Yeh paanch galtiyaan um...zu ko apna subject dene se, zu chhodne se, ya dono structures ko mix karne se hoti hain.

When a verb naturally comes with a preposition (sprechen mit, wohnen bei, kämpfen für), that preposition simply moves in front of the relative pronoun and stays there — mit dem, bei der, für den. The pronoun's CASE comes from the preposition (Dativ: mit/bei/nach/von/zu/aus; Akkusativ: für/durch/gegen/ohne/um), and its GENDER/NUMBER comes from the noun it refers back to.

Was ist ein Relativsatz mit Präposition?
When the verb requires a preposition, that preposition stays with the relative pronoun — it never moves elsewhere.
Das ist der Mann. Ich spreche mit dem Mann.
Das ist der Mann, mit dem ich spreche.
Das ist die Frau. Ich arbeite mit der Frau.
Das ist die Frau, mit der ich arbeite.
Jab verb ko preposition chahiye, woh preposition relative pronoun ke saath rehta hai — kabhi kahin aur nahi jaata.
mit, bei, nach, von, zu, aus — these common B1 prepositions always take Dativ, so their relative pronoun is dem/der/dem/denen.
Das ist der Lehrer, mit dem ich Deutsch lerne.
Das ist die Familie, bei der ich wohne.
Das ist der Kollege, von dem ich viel gelernt habe.
Das ist die Stadt, aus der ich komme.
Das ist die Universität, zu der Anna gehen möchte.
mit, bei, nach, von, zu, aus — yeh common B1 prepositions hamesha Dativ lete hain, isliye inka relative pronoun dem/der/dem/denen hota hai.
für, durch, gegen, ohne, um — these prepositions always take Akkusativ, so their relative pronoun is den/die/das/die.
Das ist der Freund, für den ich ein Geschenk gekauft habe.
Das ist die Straße, durch die wir gefahren sind.
Das ist die Entscheidung, gegen die viele Studenten protestiert haben.
für, durch, gegen, ohne, um — yeh prepositions hamesha Akkusativ lete hain, isliye inka relative pronoun den/die/das/die hota hai.

Grundstruktur: Nebensatz mit Verb am Ende
weil, da, and obwohl are all subordinating conjunctions: they introduce a subordinate clause in which the finite (conjugated) verb moves to the very end.
Structure: Hauptsatz, weil/da/obwohl + Subjekt … Verb (Satzende). Or reversed: Weil/Da/Obwohl + Subjekt … Verb, Verb + Subjekt (Hauptsatz).
Ich bin müde, weil ich lange gearbeitet habe.
Da ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause.
Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren.

weil, da, aur obwohl teeno hi subordinating conjunctions hain — inke clause mein finite verb hamesha sabse end mein jaata hai. Agar clause pehle aata hai, to comma ke baad seedha Hauptsatz ka verb aata hai (subject se pehle).
weil is the most common, most neutral way to give a reason — everyday spoken and written German. It usually follows the main clause.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten möchte.
Max war enttäuscht, weil sein Eimer weg war.
Wir bleiben zu Hause, weil es regnet.
weil sabse aam aur neutral tareeka hai reason batane ka — roz-marra ki bolchaal aur likhawat dono mein. Yeh aksar Hauptsatz ke baad aata hai.
da — der formelle, bereits bekannte Grund
da also gives a reason, but reads more formal or written, and is typically used when the reason is already known/obvious to the listener. da most often starts the sentence.
Da ich krank bin, bleibe ich heute zu Hause.
Da mein Chef den Text wollte, habe ich die ganze Nacht gearbeitet.
Da wir schon einmal dort waren, kennen wir die Wiese.
da bhi reason batata hai, par yeh zyada formal ya likhit lagta hai, aur tab aata hai jab reason pehle se pata ho. da aksar sentence ki shuruaat mein aata hai.
obwohl introduces a concessive clause: something happens despite an obstacle or expectation — the opposite of what you'd predict.
Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren.
Obwohl das stressig klingt, hast du es geschafft.
Obwohl so viel schiefgegangen ist, war die Reise toll.
obwohl contrast batata hai — kuch kisi rukawat ya ummeed ke bawajood ho jaata hai, yaani jo tum expect karte ho uska ulta.
Vergleich: weil vs. da vs. obwohl
All three change verb position identically, but their MEANING differs. Use this table to choose the right one.
Unexpected — opposite of what you'd predict

weil vs. da: both give reasons — da is not "more correct", just more formal, and often used when the reason is already obvious. weil vs. obwohl: weil explains WHY something happens; obwohl explains that something happens DESPITE a reason. da vs. obwohl: da gives a cause; obwohl gives a contrast — they can never be swapped for each other.
Teeno hi verb ko end mein bhejte hain, lekin matlab alag hai: weil = neutral reason; da = formal ya pehle se pata reason; obwohl = contrast (jo tum expect karte ho uska ulta hota hai).
These four mistakes are extremely common at B1 — usually verb position, or swapping obwohl for a reason-connector by mistake.
The finite verb (bin) must go to the very end of the weil-clause, not stay in position 2.
Same rule for da — verb to the end, not "ich bin krank".
The subject (es) comes right after obwohl; the verb (regnet) still goes to the end of that clause.
Never combine two subordinating conjunctions — pick either obwohl (contrast) or weil (reason), not both.
Sabse aam galti hai verb ko end mein na bhejna. Doosri galti hai obwohl aur weil ko ek saath jodna — hamesha sirf ek connector chuno, jo matlab ke hisaab se sahi ho.
Word order (clause at the end): Hauptsatz (Verb Position 2), [comma], weil/da/obwohl + Subjekt … Verb (Satzende).
Word order (clause first): Weil/Da/Obwohl + Subjekt … Verb (Satzende), [comma], Verb + Subjekt … (Hauptsatz — verb-second).
Are you giving a normal, everyday reason?
Are you giving a formal reason, or one the listener already knows?
Are you describing something unexpected, despite an obstacle?
Whichever connector you choose, never forget: the finite verb of that clause goes to the very end — no exceptions.

Agar clause pehle Hauptsatz ke baad ho: Hauptsatz, weil/da/obwohl + Subjekt … Verb (end mein). Agar clause pehle ho: Weil/Da/Obwohl + Subjekt … Verb, phir Verb + Subjekt (Hauptsatz, verb-second). Decision guide: (1) normal reason → weil. (2) formal ya pehle se pata reason → da. (3) koi aisi baat jo expect nahi ki jaati → obwohl.

When you narrate two past events, the one that happened FIRST needs its own marker: hatte/war + Partizip II, placed at the end of the clause. Ich hatte gegessen, bevor ich ins Kino ging. — eating happened before going to the cinema, so eating gets hatte gegessen, and going gets the normal past (ging). It's the "past before the past."

Ask yourself which of these five questions your sentence is really answering.

Temporal clauses answer: When? Before when? After when? While? All five conjunctions send the finite verb to the very end of their clause.
Ich rufe dich an, wenn ich zu Hause bin.
Temporal clauses poochte hain: Kab? Kab se pehle? Kab ke baad? Jab tak? Paanchon conjunctions finite verb ko clause ke end mein bhejte hain.
als — EIN bestimmter Zeitpunkt oder Zeitraum in der Vergangenheit

als marks ONE specific time frame in the past. That frame can be a single moment (Als Anna ankam …) or a whole period of your life (Als ich klein war …) — what matters is that you are pointing at one particular time, not at something that happens again and again. Never use als for the present or the future.
Als ich klein war, spielte ich jeden Tag Fußball.
Als Anna nach Deutschland kam, sprach sie kaum Deutsch.

als past ke ek specific time ke liye aata hai. Woh ek pal bhi ho sakta hai (Als Anna ankam …) aur zindagi ka poora daur bhi (Als ich klein war …). Dhyaan do ki us daur ke andar kaam baar-baar ho sakta hai — Als ich klein war, spielte ich jeden Tag Fußball — phir bhi als hi aayega, kyunki tum ek hi time frame ki baat kar rahe ho. Present ya future ke liye als kabhi nahi.
wenn covers repeated actions (any time frame) and any future event.
Wenn ich Zeit habe, lese ich ein Buch.
Wenn wir in Deutschland sind, besuchen wir Berlin.
wenn repeated actions (kisi bhi time frame mein) aur kisi bhi future event ko cover karta hai.
bevor marks an action that happens before another action — no special tense requirement, just plain sequencing.
Bevor ich schlafen gehe, putze ich meine Zähne.
Anna lernt Deutsch, bevor sie nach Deutschland zieht.
bevor ek action batata hai jo doosre se pehle hoti hai — koi special tense requirement nahi, bas plain sequencing.
nachdem — Handlung NACH einer anderen (oft mit Plusquamperfekt)
nachdem marks an action that happens after another — its own clause is usually in Plusquamperfekt when the main clause is Perfekt/Präteritum.
Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich spazieren.
Nachdem wir die Prüfung bestanden hatten, feierten wir zusammen.
nachdem ek action batata hai jo doosre ke baad hoti hai — iska apna clause aksar Plusquamperfekt mein hota hai jab main clause Perfekt/Präteritum ho.
während — zwei Handlungen zur gleichen Zeit
während marks two actions happening simultaneously.
Während Anna lernte, hörte Rohan Musik.
während do actions batata hai jo ek hi samay par ho rahi hon.
One question decides the conjunction every time.
Memory trick: ONE past time frame → als. EVERY time → wenn. BEFORE → bevor. AFTER → nachdem. AT THE SAME TIME → während.
Ek sawaal har baar conjunction tay kar deta hai. Past ka ek specific time? als. Baar-baar hone wali baat? wenn. Pehle? bevor. Baad mein? nachdem. Ek hi samay par? während.
These five mistakes come from confusing als/wenn, using the wrong tense with a future/past marker, or mixing up Plusquamperfekt placement.
A single, general past childhood state uses als, not wenn (wenn implies repetition each time, which doesn't fit "when I was little" as a single era).
als is never used for the future — wenn covers all future events.
Nachdem ich gegessen habe, ging ich.
Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich.
The nachdem-clause (earlier event) needs Plusquamperfekt, not Perfekt, when the main clause is in the past.
Bevor ich gegessen hatte, gehe ich duschen.
Bevor ich esse, gehe ich duschen.
bevor does not need Plusquamperfekt — plain sequencing is enough. And both halves must sit in the same time frame; Plusquamperfekt with a Präsens main clause breaks the timeline.
The finite verb (bin) must go to the very end of the während-clause, like any subordinate clause.
Yeh paanch galtiyaan als/wenn confuse karne se, galat tense use karne se, ya Plusquamperfekt placement mix karne se hoti hain.

One action, three points in time: wird repariert (Präsens — happening now), wurde repariert (Präteritum — a completed past action), and ist repariert worden (Perfekt — completed, viewed from now). A direct request in German can sound abrupt — almost like a command. Konjunktiv II softens it instantly, using the same four helper verbs every time: könnte, würde, hätte, wäre.
Öffnen Sie das Fenster. → Könnten Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
Helfen Sie mir. → Könnten Sie mir helfen?
Ich will einen Kaffee. → Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.
Direct request German mein command jaisa lag sakta hai. Konjunktiv II usko turant polite bana deta hai — hamesha yehi chaar helper verbs istemal karke: könnte, würde, hätte, wäre.
Die vier Formen: könnte, würde, hätte, wäre
You do not need to derive these forms from a rule — learn them as four fixed patterns, each attached to a Sie/du-form and (usually) a final infinitive or noun.
Asking someone to do something (softer/more formal)
Wären Sie so freundlich, das Fenster zu öffnen?
Ich würde gern einen Termin vereinbaren.
Ich würde Sie bitten, das zu wiederholen.
Inhe rule se nikaalne ki zaroorat nahi — inhe chaar fixed patterns ki tarah yaad karo, har ek Sie/du-form aur (aksar) ek infinitive ya noun ke saath aata hai.

Both ask someone to DO something. könnte focuses on ability/possibility ("could you…", asking if it's possible); würde focuses on willingness ("would you…", asking if they're willing). In everyday polite speech they are close to interchangeable — choose whichever feels natural.
Könnten Sie mir helfen? — "Could you help me?" (is it possible)
Würden Sie mir helfen? — "Would you help me?" (are you willing)

Dono hi kisi se kuch karne ke liye kehte hain, bas focus alag hai. könnte poochta hai ki tum kuch kar sakte ho ya nahi (ability), aur würde poochta hai ki tum karna chahoge ya nahi (willingness). Rozmarra bolchaal mein dono lagbhag ek jaise hi use hote hain.

Ich hätte gern … and Ich möchte … both mean "I would like…", but hätte gern is the more classically polite, slightly more formal choice for ordering or requesting a specific thing — the safest default in restaurants, shops, and offices.
Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee. (very polite, classic)
Ich möchte einen Kaffee. (polite, slightly more direct)

Ich hätte gern … aur Ich möchte … dono ka matlab hai "mujhe chahiye…", lekin hätte gern zyada classic aur formal polite tareeka hai kisi cheez ko order/request karne ka — restaurant, dukaan, office mein safest default.

These four mistakes are extremely common — mixing up plain and Konjunktiv II modal, stacking two politeness markers, or getting the word order at the end wrong.
When practising this chapter's polite pattern, use könnten (Konjunktiv II), not können (plain present) — könnten is softer and more polite.

The dative pronoun (mir) comes before the infinitive (helfen) at the end, not after it.

A quick guide for choosing the right pattern in the moment.
Need to ask politely for an action?
Need to order or request a thing?
Need to request an action, slightly softer?
Need maximum politeness for a bigger favor?
None of these patterns require you to know how Konjunktiv II is formed from scratch — learn them as fixed phrases first; the grammar behind them comes later, at B2.

der, die, das, den, dem, denen — standing alone once the noun is known. Note the plural Dativ is denen, not den, and the Genitiv pronoun is dessen/deren, never des.

Jab noun pehle se pata ho, to der/die/das/den/dem akele khade ho sakte hain. Do cheezein dhyaan mein rakho — plural Dativ mein denen aata hai (den nahi), aur Genitiv mein dessen ya deren, kabhi des nahi.
einer, eine, eines, einen, einem — the noun disappears once it's clear from context.
einer/eine/eines/einen/einem — noun gayab ho jaata hai jab context se saaf ho.
meiner, deiner, seiner, ihrer, unserer, eurer (or meins/deins for neuter Nom./Akk.) — standing alone as possessive pronouns.
meiner/deiner/seiner/ihrer/unserer/eurer (ya meins/deins) — akele khade possessive pronoun ke roop mein.
dieser/diese/dieses and jener/jene/jenes — standing alone, pointing at something already mentioned or visible.
dieser/diese/dieses aur jener/jene/jenes — akele khade, kisi pehle se mentioned cheez ki taraf ishaara karte hue.

Was ist ein Partizip als Adjektiv?
A participle can describe a noun just like an adjective, and declines exactly the same way.
Ek participle noun ko bilkul adjective ki tarah describe kar sakta hai, aur waisa hi decline hota hai.
Verb stem + -end. Describes someone/something ACTIVELY doing the action.
Verb stem + -end. Kisi ko active roop se action karte hue describe karta hai.
The familiar Perfekt participle, now used as an adjective. Describes the RESULT of an action.
Wahi jaana-pehchaana Perfekt participle, ab ek adjective ke roop mein. Action ke RESULT ko describe karta hai.
Partizip I = active, ongoing. Partizip II = passive/result, completed.
der schlafende Hund — the dog IS sleeping
der geschlossene Laden — the shop HAS BEEN closed
Partizip I = active, chal raha hai. Partizip II = result, ho chuka hai.
Participle adjectives follow the exact same declension rules as ordinary adjectives — weak, mixed, or strong.
Participle adjectives bilkul ordinary adjectives ki tarah decline hote hain — weak, mixed, ya strong.

You already know how to give a REASON (weil, da). Now add the RESULT. deshalb states a plain result — and the finite verb comes immediately after it: Es regnet. Deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause. so … dass shows just how STRONG that result was: Ich war so nervös, dass ich alles vergessen habe. Three levels, one logic: Cause (weil/da) → Result (deshalb) → Strong Result (so … dass).

You already know how to give a REASON with weil and da. This chapter adds the next step: the RESULT of that reason.
Structure: Satz 1 (Ursache). Deshalb + Verb + Subjekt … (Satz 2, Ergebnis).
Ich habe Fieber. Deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
Es regnet. Deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause.

Tumhe pehle se pata hai ki weil aur da se reason kaise batate hain. Yeh chapter agla step sikhata hai: us reason ka result. deshalb ke turant baad verb aata hai, phir subject.

deshalb is NOT a subordinating conjunction — it simply occupies the front position of its own sentence. That means the finite verb comes IMMEDIATELY after deshalb (verb-second word order), never the subject.
Deshalb bin ich glücklich. (verb immediately after deshalb)
Deshalb ich bin glücklich. (wrong — subject cannot come before the verb here)
Both word orders work: separate sentences — Es regnet. Deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause. — or joined with a comma — Es regnet, deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause.

Use so + Adjektiv + …, dass … when something is so strong/extreme that another event becomes its direct consequence. The finite verb of the dass-clause goes to the very end, just like weil/da/obwohl.

viel stays viel (no plural -e) with uncountable/mass nouns; viele takes the plural ending with countable nouns.

Rule of thumb: one-syllable masculine/neuter nouns and those ending in -s, -ß, -z, -sch often take -es (des Mannes); longer masculine/neuter nouns usually take just -s (des Autos, des Lehrers).
Masculine aur neuter nouns Genitiv mein -s ya -es lagate hain. Feminine aur plural nouns par koi ending nahi lagti — sirf article badalta hai.
wegen means "because of" and always takes the Genitiv. It states a REASON.
Wegen des Regens bleiben wir zu Hause.
Wegen der Krankheit kommt Anna nicht.
Wegen des Verkehrs bin ich zu spät.
Wegen meiner Prüfung lerne ich heute viel.
wegen ka matlab hai "ki wajah se" aur hamesha Genitiv leta hai. Yeh reason batata hai.
trotz means "despite, in spite of" and always takes the Genitiv. It states an unexpected CONTRAST — something happens anyway.
Trotz des Regens gehen wir spazieren.
Trotz der Probleme arbeitet er weiter.
Trotz der Müdigkeit lernt sie Deutsch.
trotz ka matlab hai "ke bawajood" aur hamesha Genitiv leta hai. Yeh contrast batata hai — rukawat ke bawajood kuch phir bhi ho jaata hai.
während means "during" and always takes the Genitiv. Something happens WHILE another action or period is going on.
Während des Unterrichts darf man nicht telefonieren.
Während der Reise haben wir viele Fotos gemacht.
Während des Essens sprechen wir Deutsch.
während ka matlab hai "ke dauran" aur hamesha Genitiv leta hai. Kuch tab hota hai jab koi doosra kaam ya samay chal raha hota hai.
wegen vs. trotz vs. während — Vergleich
All three take the Genitiv, but each does a different job.
Teeno hi Genitiv lete hain, lekin har ek ka kaam alag hai — wegen (reason), trotz (bawajood), während (ke dauran).
Different prepositions require different cases — memorise them prepositon by preposition rather than by a general rule.
mit dem Lehrer (Dativ) vs. wegen des Lehrers (Genitiv)
für den Lehrer (Akkusativ) vs. trotz des Lehrers (Genitiv)
In casual spoken German, wegen and trotz are sometimes heard with the Dativ ("wegen dem Regen") — but for this chapter's written/formal B1 register, always use the Genitiv.

Alag-alag prepositions alag cases maangte hain — inhe ek-ek karke yaad rakho, kisi general rule se nahi. Bolchaal mein kabhi-kabhi wegen/trotz ke saath Dativ sunayi deta hai, lekin is chapter ke liye hamesha Genitiv use karo.
These mistakes are extremely common at B1 — using the Dativ instead of the Genitiv, or forgetting the noun's Genitiv ending.
wegen takes the Genitiv (des Regens), not the Dativ (dem Regen), in this chapter's formal register.
trotz takes the Genitiv plural (der Probleme), not the Dativ plural (den Problemen).
während takes the Genitiv (des Unterrichts), not the Akkusativ (den Unterricht).
Masculine nouns need both the Genitiv article (des) AND the noun ending (-es): des Mannes.
Neuter nouns still need the Genitiv -s ending on the noun itself: des Autos.
Masculine nouns need the Genitiv -s ending: des Lehrers.
Sabse aam galtiyaan: Dativ ka istemal Genitiv ki jagah karna, ya noun ki Genitiv ending bhool jaana. Hamesha article AUR noun ending dono check karo.
For the Goethe exam: the Genitiv shows up constantly in formal writing and reading passages — recognising it quickly (des/der + noun ending) speeds up comprehension.
Memory trick: Wessen? → Genitiv. wegen → Reason. trotz → Despite. während → During.

Goethe exam ke liye: Genitiv formal likhawat aur reading passages mein baar-baar aata hai — ise jaldi pehchaanna (des/der + noun ending) samajhne mein madad karta hai. Yaad rakhne ka tarika: Wessen? → Genitiv. wegen → reason. trotz → bawajood. während → ke dauran.
The story of an old settlement
während + Genitiv states a time period.

Because of the great poverty, a merchant family decided to build a social housing project. Because of the family's Catholic faith, the project was oriented toward charity. Despite the low endowment capital, the settlement could be built. A night watchman guarded the apartments during the night. Because of the buildings' good original condition, the settlement is touristically interesting today.

A first verb (hoffen, versuchen, vergessen, planen, vorhaben, versprechen…), an adjective construction (Es ist wichtig …), or a noun construction (Ich habe Lust …) all link to a second verb with zu + Infinitiv at the end. Separable verbs insert zu between the prefix and the stem: anzurufen, mitzubringen.
Es ist wichtig, genug zu schlafen.
Ich habe Lust, ins Kino zu gehen.
Pehla verb, adjective construction, ya noun construction sabhi zu + Infinitiv se doosre verb ko end mein jodte hain. Trennbare verbs mein zu prefix aur verb ke beech mein aata hai.
All three send the finite verb to the very end of their clause. weil is the neutral, everyday reason; da is the more formal/already-known reason; obwohl signals an unexpected contrast.
Ich bin müde, weil ich gearbeitet habe.
Da ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause.
Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren.
Teeno hi apne clause ke end mein finite verb bhejte hain. weil neutral reason deta hai, da formal ya pehle se pata reason, aur obwohl contrast batata hai.
könnte/würde soften a request for an action; hätte gern requests a thing; wäre so freundlich reaches for maximum politeness. Never combine two of these markers in one clause.
Wären Sie so freundlich, das Fenster zu öffnen?
könnte/würde ek action ke liye request ko soft karte hain; hätte gern ek cheez ke liye; wäre so freundlich sabse zyada politeness ke liye. Do markers ko kabhi ek saath mat jodo.
deshalb states a plain result and pulls the finite verb immediately after it. so + Adjektiv/viel/viele + dass shows a strong consequence, with the dass-clause verb at the end.
Es regnet. Deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause.
Ich war so müde, dass ich sofort eingeschlafen bin.
deshalb ek plain result batata hai aur uske turant baad verb aata hai. so + Adjektiv/viel/viele + dass ek strong consequence dikhata hai.
The Genitiv answers Wessen? (Whose?). wegen states a reason, trotz a contrast, während a time period — all three always take the Genitiv.

The Präteritum is the same past as the Perfekt you already know — but with a different register. Spoken German reaches for the Perfekt: Ich bin nach Hause gegangen. Written German — stories, newspapers, biographies — reaches for the Präteritum: Ich ging nach Hause. Two exceptions apply everywhere, spoken or written: sein (war) and haben (hatte) almost always appear in the Präteritum, even in conversation — and so do the modal verbs (konnte, musste, wollte…).

Perfekt vs. Präteritum — dieselbe Vergangenheit, anderes Register

Both tenses describe the past — they don't differ in meaning, only in register. Perfekt dominates spoken German. Präteritum dominates written German: stories, books, newspapers, reports, formal writing, narration.
Ich bin nach Hause gegangen. (Perfekt — spoken)
Dono tenses past ko describe karte hain — matlab mein fark nahi, register mein hai. Perfekt bolchaal mein zyada, Präteritum likhawat mein zyada (kahaniyaan, akhbaar, report, formal writing).
sein almost always appears in the Präteritum — even in spoken German.
sein lagbhag hamesha Präteritum mein aata hai — bolchaal mein bhi.
Like sein, haben almost always appears in the Präteritum, in speech and writing alike.
sein ki tarah, haben bhi lagbhag hamesha Präteritum mein aata hai — bolchaal aur likhawat dono mein.
Modal verbs are used VERY often in the Präteritum instead of the Perfekt — this is normal and expected, even in spoken German.

German time expressions come in two flavours: everyday Dativ expressions you use constantly in speech, and literary/formal Genitiv expressions common in stories, newspapers, and Goethe B1 reading texts.
am Montag (everyday Dativ) vs. eines Tages (literary Genitiv)

German time expressions do tarah ke hote hain: everyday Dativ jo bolchaal mein hamesha use hota hai, aur literary/formal Genitiv jo kahaniyon, akhbaaron, aur Goethe B1 reading mein aam hai.
Most everyday time expressions use the Dativ, contracted with an/in: am (an dem) for weekdays and parts of the day; im (in dem) for seasons and months; in der for night.

Zyada tar everyday time expressions Dativ use karte hain, an/in ke saath contract hoke: am (weekdays, din ke hisse), im (seasons, mahine), in der (raat).
These formal, story-like expressions are common in narration, newspapers, and Goethe B1 reading — masculine/neuter nouns need the -s/-es ending, feminine nouns need none.
eines Tages / Morgens / Abends / Nachts / Jahres
one day / morning / evening / night / year

at the end of the year

The six most common B1 time prepositions, each with its required case.
Yeh chhe B1 time prepositions har ek apna case maangte hain: während (Genitiv), vor/nach/seit/ab (Dativ), bis (Akkusativ ya bina case).
These five mistakes are extremely common at B1 — dropping the Genitiv ending, using the wrong case with Anfang/Ende/Mitte, or mixing am/im with the wrong time category.
der Tag is masculine — it needs the Genitiv -s ending: eines Tages.
Anfang takes the Genitiv (des), not the Dativ (dem).
das Jahr is neuter, so its Genitiv article is des, not den.
Weekdays take am (an dem), not im (in dem).
Seasons take im (in dem), not am (an dem).
